title: Employment Verification Letter: 3 Free Templates and What to Include
summary: Three copy-paste employment verification letter templates — a standard third-party letter, a proof of income letter for landlords, and a lender-ready VOE built around Fannie Mae Form 1005 — plus the fields every letter needs and the two errors that invalidate most letters.
body_text: An employment verification letter is a short document on company letterhead that confirms an employee's job title, dates of employment, and employment status — plus income, when the employee has authorized that disclosure in writing. This page gives you three free copy-paste employment verification letter templates, one for each requester you'll actually hear from: a standard third-party letter, a proof of income letter for landlords, and a mortgage-ready VOE letter built around Fannie Mae Form 1005. TL;DR This guide gives you three copy-paste employment verification letter templates, each built for a specific requester: Standard third-party letter for agencies, other employers, and government requesters who need job title, dates, and status confirmed. Proof of income letter for landlords and property managers screening a tenant, where salary or income confirmation is the point. Verification of employment letter for mortgage and lending underwriters, who expect letterhead, base salary, and a direct verifier contact. Two errors invalidate more letters than anything else. Missing or unverifiable employer contact information kills the callback step, and disclosing salary without written authorization exposes you to a compliance problem. If you handle these requests at volume, a section further down covers outsourcing the outreach directly rather than drafting each letter by hand. What is an employment verification letter, and when do you need one? An employment verification letter confirms a few narrow facts about a person's employment for a third party who needs to trust them. It states that someone works or worked for you, their job title, and their dates of employment, sometimes with income if the employee has authorized that disclosure. A reference letter, by contrast, offers opinions about performance and fit, and a background check report pulls together criminal, credit, and other records from outside sources. The verification letter stays factual and stays inside what your own records can prove. Three requests account for nearly all the letters HR teams write. A third party such as a staffing agency, another employer, or a government office asks for basic confirmation of employment. A landlord or property manager asks for proof that a rental applicant earns enough to cover rent. A mortgage lender or underwriter asks for detailed employment and income facts to approve a loan. The three templates below map directly to those requests. Who signs the letter matters as much as what it says. Most verifiers expect an HR representative, a direct manager, or a designated verifier whose contact information they can call back to confirm the letter is real. Authorization matters just as much. You should have the employee's written consent before releasing anything beyond title and dates, since salary and other sensitive fields can trigger state disclosure and salary-history restrictions if you share them without permission. What should an employment verification letter include — and leave out? Letter type Confirms Typical requester Standard third-party Job title, dates, employment status Staffing agencies, other employers, government offices Tenant screening Job title, dates, and income (with authorization) Landlords, property managers Mortgage/lending Job title, dates, base salary, employment type, continuance Loan officers, underwriters Four fields belong in every verification letter regardless of who asks. State the employee's job title, their dates of employment, whether they are currently active or separated, and a way for the verifier to reach your company directly. A verifier reads those four items to confirm the person worked where they claim, for as long as they claim, in the role they claim. Leave one out and the letter bounces back with a follow-up question, which restarts the clock. Salary and reason for leaving are conditional. Do not include either unless the employee has authorized it or the request itself carries proper authorization. Several states restrict how salary history gets disclosed, so releasing pay figures without written consent creates exposure you do not want. When a landlord or lender needs income, confirm you have the authorization in hand before typing a number, not after. Formatting is what separates a letter a verifier trusts from one they treat as suspect. Put the letter on company letterhead, date it, and sign it with a real name and title rather than a generic signature block. Include a direct callback number that reaches a person who can confirm the details, not a general switchboard. Verifiers almost always call to confirm, and a letter that routes them to a dead-end line reads as unverifiable even when every fact in it is correct. Keep the dates consistent with what your payroll and HR systems show. A start date on the letter that disagrees with the record a background screener pulls independently triggers a follow-up call at minimum, and can put the whole letter under closer scrutiny. Pull the numbers straight from your system of record before you draft, so nothing in the letter contradicts what a verifier finds when they check. Standard third-party employment verification letter template Most verification requests you field are the generic kind. A staffing agency, another employer running a pre-hire check, or a government office confirming eligibility for benefits sends a request, and all they need is confirmation that the person worked for you, in what role, and for how long. No salary, no income figures, no separate authorization required unless the requester specifically asks and the employee has consented. This is the letter to reach for when someone just wants proof the employment relationship existed. Because it omits income, this version carries the least compliance risk of the three. You can send it on a standard confirmation of job title, dates, and current status without triggering salary-history restrictions that vary by state. Keep it short. A verifier scanning dozens of these a day wants the facts and a callback number, not a narrative. Requests like this one are exactly what Superunit's verification service handles directly for employers, so you can send this template yourself for a one-off request, or route repeat requests to Superunit once the volume stops being occasional. Copy the template below and replace the bracketed fields. [Company Letterhead] [Date] To Whom It May Concern, This letter confirms the employment of [Employee Full Name] with [Company Name]. Job Title: [Current or Most Recent Job Title] Employment Status: [Full-time / Part-time / Contract] Dates of Employment: [Start Date] to [End Date or "Present"] [Employee Full Name] remains employed with our organization as of the date of this letter. / [Employee Full Name] was employed with our organization for the dates listed above. If you require further verification, please contact me directly using the information below. We can only release additional details, including compensation, with the employee's written authorization. Sincerely, [Verifier Name] [Title] [Company Name] [Direct Phone Number] [Email Address] The direct phone number does the real work here. It lets the requester close the loop by callback, which most third parties treat as the actual confirmation step, more than anything printed above it. The authorization line backs that up by making clear that salary and other sensitive details stay locked until the employee signs off. Keep both even when the current request looks simple, since the same requester often comes back asking for more. Prefer a formatted file? The download mirrors the plain text above, with a letterhead band you can swap for your own and a before-sending checklist to delete once the fields are filled. Download the standard letter template (.docx) Proof of income letter for tenant screening requests Landlords and property managers ask for income confirmation because most run applicants against an affordability rule of thumb, commonly rent at or below roughly a third of gross monthly income, though the exact ratio varies by landlord and market. A generic verification letter that only confirms job title and dates fails that test, because the reviewer cannot check the ratio without a salary figure. When you write for this audience, lead with the income detail they will actually calculate against. State income as a specific number tied to a pay period, and match it to how the applicant reported it on the rental application. A screener comparing your letter to a paystub or the applicant's stated income will flag any gap, so confirm annual base salary or an hourly rate with typical scheduled hours rather than a vague "competitive compensation" phrase. If the applicant listed variable pay like commission or bonuses, note whether that income is regular or discretionary, since landlords weigh guaranteed income differently. Disclosure authorization sets the boundary here. Some states and cities restrict what an employer can say about salary history, and you should confirm the applicant has signed a release covering income before you put a dollar figure in writing. When you have that release, name the field plainly. When you do not, confirm employment and status only, and note that salary can follow once written authorization is on file. That single line protects you from disclosing compensation the applicant never agreed to share. Employment stability matters as much as the number. Landlords are underwriting a year or more of rent, so state whether the role is full-time, part-time, or seasonal, and confirm the employment start date so the reviewer can gauge tenure. If the position is at-will with no defined end, say so directly rather than implying permanence you cannot promise. Plain-text template Copy the block below and replace every bracketed field. Keep it on company letterhead with a dated signature and a direct callback number for the verifier. [Company letterhead] [Date] To Whom It May Concern, This letter confirms that [Employee Full Name] is currently employed by [Company Name] as a [Job Title], with a start date of [Start Date]. Their employment status is [Full-Time / Part-Time / Seasonal]. With the employee's written authorization, we confirm gross compensation of [$Amount] per [year / hour], based on [Scheduled Hours, if hourly]. [Note any regular variable income here, or delete.] Direct questions to [Verifier Name], [Title], at [Phone] or [Email]. Sincerely, [Signature, Name, Title] If you'd rather work from a formatted file, the same letter is available as a download. The plain-text block above stays the primary copy-paste artifact on this page. Download the proof of income letter template (.docx) Verification of employment letter for mortgage and lending underwriting Mortgage underwriters read verification letters more closely than any other requester, and a letter that satisfies a landlord will often bounce back from a loan file. Underwriters have to defend every income figure they put into a debt-to-income calculation, so they want language that leaves no room for interpretation. A vague phrase like "earns a competitive salary" is useless to them. They need the exact base salary, the pay frequency, and whether the figure is guaranteed or variable. Base salary draws the closest scrutiny, stated as an annual or hourly figure with the pay period spelled out, so the underwriter can convert it cleanly into monthly qualifying income. Employment type matters almost as much, since full-time, part-time, contract, and seasonal work all get treated differently in a debt-to-income calculation. Likelihood of continued employment sounds like a soft detail, but a letter that stays silent on it can trigger a follow-up call anyway, because underwriters want some signal that the borrower's income will persist through the life of the loan. Because a lender may resell the loan, the letter usually needs to sit on company letterhead with a dated signature and a direct callback number for the person who signed it. A general HR line that routes to a queue slows the file down. Underwriters call to confirm, and they want to reach the named verifier without navigating a phone tree. Many conventional lenders use or reference Fannie Mae Form 1005 , the standard Verification of Employment form, as the format their underwriters expect. You do not have to complete the 1005 itself to satisfy a request, but a free-text letter should cover the same fields the form captures. If your letter includes current and past base pay, employment dates, position, hours, employment type, and a note on continuance, it can substitute cleanly in the loan file without a second request. [Employee Name] has been employed with [Company Name] since [Start Date] in the position of [Job Title], on a [full-time / part-time] basis. Their current base salary is [$Amount] per [year / hour], paid [pay frequency]. Based on current business conditions, we have no reason to anticipate a change in their employment status. For verification, contact [Verifier Name] at [Direct Phone] or [Email]. Signed, [Verifier Name, Title], [Date]. The download below is a formatted version of this letter built to mirror the 1005 fields, so you can hand underwriters a document they recognize on sight. Download the mortgage VOE letter template (.docx) What mistakes delay or invalidate an employment verification letter? Most rejected verification letters fail for the same handful of reasons, and each carries a real cost to the person waiting on it. Missing or unverifiable employer contact information stalls letters more than any other defect. A verifier who cannot reach a live person to confirm the letter treats it as unverified, which means a mortgage file sits until the underwriter gets a callback and a rental application moves to the next candidate. Put a direct phone number that reaches someone who can confirm the details, not a general HR mailbox or a switchboard that dead-ends in voicemail. Unauthorized salary disclosure creates the opposite problem. Instead of delaying the request, it exposes you. Many states and cities restrict how employers can share compensation, and some tie salary disclosure to written authorization from the employee. When a letter lists salary without that authorization on file, you have handed the requester grounds to challenge the process and the employee grounds to complain. Confirm you have signed authorization before any number goes in the letter, and leave salary out entirely when the request does not require it. Inconsistent dates are the quiet failure. Your HR system, your payroll system, and the manager's memory often disagree by a few weeks on a hire or termination date. A landlord comparing your letter to a pay stub or a lender cross-checking against tax records will flag the mismatch and ask for a corrected letter, which restarts the clock. Pull dates from the system of record, usually payroll, and verify them against the request before you sign. Each of these sends the requester back for a second letter. Auditing for all three before you send costs a few minutes and spares you the repeat request, the delayed closing, or the rejected application that follows a sloppy one. After the letter is sent: what verifiers do next Sending the letter rarely ends the request. Most verifiers on the receiving end will not accept a letter at face value. They call the number on the letterhead, confirm the details with a live person, and note the date and name of whoever answered. A phone call is harder to fake than a printed letter, so lenders and screeners treat that conversation as the real verification and the letter as supporting paper. That callback is where your HR time actually goes. Drafting a template takes minutes. Fielding the follow-up calls, pulling up the employee's record again, and confirming dates and title on the spot pulls someone away from other work, and the calls arrive without warning. The cost compounds for any employer with real headcount. A single former employee can generate a landlord check, a mortgage verification, and a CRA request inside the same month, each with its own callback. Multiply that across everyone who rents, buys, or changes jobs, and confirmation calls become a steady background load that no template removes. When it's faster to let Superunit handle verification requests than draft them yourself Once a single HR person is fielding verification requests for a few hundred employees, drafting letters by hand stops being a reasonable use of anyone's time. The letter itself takes ten minutes. The callback confirmation, the voicemail tag, the second request when the first letter had a stale end date, and the landlord who insists on speaking to a live verifier are what eat the afternoon. Superunit is an AI outreach service that runs employment and income verification for you across phone, email, and fax, as a direct vendor rather than a database or software subscription, so you stop being the phone line for every agency, landlord, and lender that asks. The narrow-scope argument is the one worth making plainly. When a lender or property manager asks only for confirmation of employment and income, buying a full background-check package is the wrong tool. You do not need criminal records, credit pulls, or a bundled report priced for a hiring decision. You need one fact confirmed and documented. Superunit does verification-only outreach across phone, email, and fax, scoped to exactly what the request asks for and nothing more. The same approach applies whether you're fielding an inbound request from a CRA or lender or initiating verification yourself. The mechanism is straightforward. You hand off the incoming request, Superunit's AI reaches the requester on whatever channel they prefer, confirms the authorized fields, and returns a documented result you can drop into the file. Because the outreach runs across all three channels at once, a mortgage underwriter who only accepts faxed confirmations and a landlord who wants a callback get handled the same day without you touching either. That documentation matters if a dispute ever surfaces. An audit trail showing who was contacted, on which channel, and what was confirmed is exactly what a screener or lender needs to defend the file under FCRA recordkeeping requirements. This is not a free routing tool that forwards requests to a CRA. You hire Superunit to run the verification workflow itself, and the capacity does not depend on your headcount. When request volume spikes during leasing season or a refinancing wave, outsourced verification outreach absorbs it without you hiring a temp to answer the phone. FAQ Can an employer refuse to provide a verification letter? In most states, no law forces a private employer to issue a verification letter, so refusal is legally permitted in many cases. Employers responding to third-party requests still tend to comply because ignoring lender or landlord verifications strands their own current and former employees. Setting a consistent response policy avoids the appearance of retaliating against specific people. Is salary required by law? Salary disclosure is not legally required, and several states restrict what you can share about prior compensation, so you should confirm the specific request against your state's salary-history rules. Include compensation only when the employee has authorized it or the requester has provided signed consent. When in doubt, verify employment dates and status alone. How long should a verification letter take to process? A standard letter takes a few minutes to draft once you confirm the details against your HR records. Turnaround stretches when a verifier follows up by phone to confirm the letter, which is where volume slows HR teams down. Publishing a direct callback number on the letter cuts that lag. Does the letter need to be notarized? Notarization is rarely required for routine employment or income verification. Lenders and landlords generally accept a dated letter on company letterhead with a signature and a working callback number. Confirm the specific requester's format expectations before sending. Three templates for one-off letters, Superunit for volume The three templates above cover almost every one-off request you'll get. Copy the standard version for agencies and other employers, the income variant for landlords, and the lender version when it needs to match a Fannie Mae Form 1005. Fill in the brackets, check the contact details and dates, and send. The templates stop being enough when the requests stop being occasional. If CRAs, landlords, and lenders are hitting you across dozens of employees, drafting and confirming each one by hand turns into a standing job. At that point a defined process handles what templates can't, whether you build it in-house or hand the outreach to Superunit to run across phone, email, and fax.

title: NTP Security
body_text: Executive Summary There are just a few internet system services that practically every internet host uses on a regular basis. The Network Time Protocol (NTP), perhaps little known to the average user, is just one such system. However, some NTP systems have been abused to facilitate reflection and amplification (RA) distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. And because NTP is so widespread and critical, any vulnerabilities in the system are worrying. NTP-based attacks and scanning for abuseable systems is an ongoing phenomenon. So far in 2025, we have seen more than 45,000 DDoS alerts where NTP was involved as reflectors. Compared with the hundreds of thousands of attacks we see over the same time frame, this is a relatively small proportion. However, we ignore and underestimate this activity at our peril. This report looks at the current state of NTP scanning in the wild, the potentially abuseable NTP systems still in operation on the public internet, the current landscape of NTP packet-flooding attacks, and patterns defenders should know about to detect and mitigate unwanted NTP activity. Key Findings NTP remains one of the most ubiquitous, widely used subsystems on the internet. Legitimate NTP traffic has specific patterns, payloads, and packet-size profiles. Relatively few hosting providers make up the bulk of unsolicited NTP activity. Background NTP is one of the internet’s longest-running protocol systems. It is also one of the most widely deployed and used services. NTP is present and active on the largest internet servers, down to the smallest handheld devices you might find in your pocket. Its job is to help ensure a system has an accurate notion of time by performing periodic synchronization exchanges to one or more time servers. It performs this feat via a series of well-structured messages running on top of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). NTP is widely used and critical for all sorts of applications, ranging from authentication to logging. Unfortunately, many UDP-based applications, such as DNS, RIPv1, SNMP, and NTP, have been susceptible to spoofed source reflection attacks. The NTP-specific threat derives from a number of management functions built into the protocol that historically required no authentication. For example, the “monlist” command, if supported, could return a cached list of NTP clients, their source IP address, and their port number to anyone who asks by using a small, single UDP datagram. For popular NTP servers, such a query could result in many full-size UDP datagrams being returned. Monlist or related capabilities have made NTP a favorite DDoS attack vector because there originally were hundreds of thousands of abuseable systems when this capability for DDoS was first recognized more than 10 years ago. Fortunately, the number of reflection/amplification (R/A) attacks involving NTP has been decreasing as software and operations have tended toward better defaults and best practices.[1] Nevertheless, the threat of abuseable NTP servers has not been completely eradicated. Interestingly, unlike with many other protocols, there are very clear and specific traffic characteristics that differentiate unwanted NTP traffic from the rest. We explore these differences here to help operators better understand their own NTP traffic patterns and ultimately help mitigate unwanted NTP-related traffic. NTP Activity Analysis In the following three subsections, we consider internet NTP activity from three distinct vantage points. First, we detail the behavior of NTP scanners in the wild. Using a sample of traffic seen at our sensors, we summarize what third-party scanners are doing and how they are doing it. Second, we look at the responses to internet NTP scanning. Our team conducts low-impact internetwide NTP scans to detect abuseable systems on the internet. We share the results with our customers to enhance their DDoS defense capabilities. Third, we summarize recent NTP-specific attack alerts that we see from our own DDoS activity intelligence. Together, these three perspectives help paint a more complete picture of the NTP traffic threat landscape. NTP Scanners Our investigation starts with NETSCOUT honeypots, configured as low-interaction systems that capture but do not serve content. We recorded UDP messages to UDP destination port 123 and analyzed what we found. Our honeypots see primarily three broad categories of unsolicited NTP messages called “modes.” The mode is encoded in a 3-bit NTP header field. The most common value we see is mode 7. This corresponds to a private-use or implementation-specific NTP message type. In practice, the reference NTP.org implementation uses this mode for a variety of management functions. It is mode 7 where the infamous “monlist” function is found. Monlist, if supported, instructs an NTP service to return a cached list of other NTP endpoints that have communicated with the system. This list can be quite large, and because a single source address–spoofed packet can solicit the response, this feature has been widely abused in reflection/amplification attacks. The next most common NTP packet types we see are mode 3, which corresponds to client time-synchronization messages. Mode 3 packets and their responses, with few exceptions for local management traffic, are the only NTP communication you’d normally expect to see on a network. Mode 3 requests and responses are effectively small packets of equal, fixed size. They convey the information necessary for one system to synchronize its clock with a high degree of precision to another by using encoded time stamps and round-trip time estimations. These packets generally pose relatively little risk, even when unsolicited. Usually, we find sources of this traffic originating from legitimate threat intelligence and research NTP surveying systems. However, if you have a system that will respond to unsolicited mode 3 time-synchronization requests, this may be an early warning that someone is cataloging your network or fingerprinting accessible systems. There are many open NTP servers on the internet where this activity is warranted, but you should be sure you want your servers to be among them before allowing them to reply to clock-synchronization messages from anywhere or anyone. The only other NTP mode we see in any measurable amount is mode 6 messages. NTP mode 6 packets are defined as control messages, having more in common with NTP.org’s mode 7 usage than mode 3 messages. In practice, NTP.org is the only widely deployed implementation that has supported both mode 6 and 7 messages by default. Unlike mode 3 messages, both mode 6 and 7 messages can be abused for R/A attacks. They can also leak information about the system that you may otherwise wish to limit (e.g., operating system version information and software configuration settings). The sources of scans for each mode vary, but most activity we see originates from legitimate NTP research and surveyor projects. However, there are a number of sources that are more suspicious. Sometimes these originate from little-known hosting providers; other times they originate from systems we wouldn’t expect to see unsolicited traffic from (e.g., a country with which we would rarely expect to exchange traffic). Some may even be spoofed, but we see little evidence of that behavior at our honeypots. NTP Responders Our low-impact vulnerability scanning service looks to identify abuseable NTP systems on the internet. We examined responses to a recent scan on the IPv4 internet. There are multiple techniques to NTP scanning, but here we consider only responses to a special “mode 7” request commonly referred to as “GET_MONLIST.” This is the special management query used by the reference NTP implementation. If available and permitted, the NTP server will respond with a list of client systems it has communicated with, stored in a local cache. A valid response suggests that the NTP responder is susceptible to R/A attacks, although some responses may be from third-party NTP honeypots in the wild. There are many NTP servers on the internet, but we are particularly interested in those that may contribute to R/A attacks. At one time, the number of abuseable NTP systems was measured in hundreds of thousands. Fortunately, the vast majority of vulnerable systems have been updated or removed from service. We now measure them in the mere thousands. We'd like this number to effectively be zero, but compared with other threat vectors, NTP going from one of the biggest populations of amplifiers to one this small is a net positive. The reduction in vulnerable NTP systems was a result of broad community recognition and cooperation to mitigate the problem. Our surveying turns up a diverse set of networks, meaning we find no one set of networks is responsible for the majority of vulnerable systems. Some systems may even be other honeypots unknown to us, masking a lower bound of the threat population. We continue to report on those we find vulnerable and include them in our regularly updated threat intelligence feeds. The reason for this will become obvious as we detail it in the next section. NTP DDoS Attacks Despite the significant decline in the number of vulnerable NTP systems used in DDoS attacks, we still find a surprising number of attack alerts where NTP is involved. So far this year, for example, we have seen more than 45,000 attack alerts with an NTP traffic component. About one-fourth (12,000) of those attack alerts were triggered by our NTP attack detection logic. These numbers seem to far exceed what we’d expect given the population of systems we see from scanning. There are reasonable explanations for this seemingly unlikely discrepancy. One possibility is that NTP attacks have been part of the miscreant DDoS toolkit for a long time, and they remain popular with some attack kits, while the number of vulnerable systems continues to be abused rather than fixed. Another is that NTP attacks we see may not always be reflections from amplifiers we look for, but just UDP floods from direct-path sources. In some uncommon but devastatingly harmful cases, we have also seen device manufacturers set NTP servers to hard-coded IP addresses of unwitting third parties. If these devices proliferate or if the third party renumbers, otherwise uninteresting time-synchronization traffic can pose significant problems to those not expecting it. NTP Traffic Profiling One of the little secrets about NTP is how little legitimate traffic fluctuates in normal operations. Nowadays, we rarely see anything but mode 3 packets in legitimate operations, and those packets are practically always the same size in both directions (i.e., 48 bytes of UPD payload). Knowing a certain class of traffic (e.g., UDP port 123) should only ever be a specific length can significantly aid in monitoring and filtering actions. When we know what is normal, what is not, and what we might wish to allow, we can more effectively mitigate traffic that does not fit the expected profile. Very few protocols and applications behave this way in practice. Beware, however: This is not guaranteed to be true in every environment. There are scenarios where NTP behavior may show variation to these rules, so do not carelessly make simple assumptions or impose traffic rules until you’ve meticulously studied your own environment for outliers. Even if you cannot rely on NTP traffic to behave exactly as we describe 100 percent of the time, in extreme situations when an attack exhibits lots of unusual NTP traffic patterns, the common case can be used in emergency situations temporarily. Recommendations To detect and mitigate abusive, ever-changing networks of varying size and duration, we recommend the following: Real-time visibility into volumetric traffic floods and distributed attack patterns. Tools such as NETSCOUT Arbor Sightline can help surface early signs of trouble and trigger flow-specification and remotely triggered black hole (RTBH) defenses to upstream providers. Proactive mitigation with automated systems such as Arbor Threat Mitigation System (TMS) or Arbor Edge Defense (AED) . These can stop both volumetric floods and more-complex multivector attacks. Intelligence-driven defense with feeds such as NETSCOUT’s ATLAS Intelligence Feed (AIF) . These provide information about context, what’s trending, who’s being targeted, and how actors are evolving. Staying ahead of threat actors is an ever-changing job and requires a broad view of where these attacks come from, how they operate, and where they could strike next. Conclusion Due to the very ubiquity of NTP services on the internet, we keep a pulse on what is normal and expected behavior year after year. At one time, DDoS attacks stemming from vulnerable NTP systems were among the most frequent and powerful threat vectors in an adversary’s arsenal. Today, NTP systems are more resilient and less susceptible to abuse than they once were. The threat has not been eliminated, however, and we continue to see abuse stemming from vulnerable NTP systems regularly. The good news is the frequency and impact has waned. Furthermore, mitigation techniques are available, and realizing how normal NTP traffic behaves can help further reduce future threats. NTP is one of the few protocols that is so widespread but predictable in how it behaves. We use these features to our advantage to protect against not only today’s threats, but also tomorrow’s. title: Stationary Bike vs Treadmill: Home Buyer's Guide
summary: Stationary bike vs treadmill for home? Compare calories, joint impact, muscles, space, and noise, plus the one factor that decides which you'll actually use.
body_text: Stationary Bike vs Treadmill: An Honest Home Buyer's Guide Two great machines. The real question is which one you will still be using in six months. For most people buying one machine for home, a stationary bike wins on joint-friendliness, quiet, and small footprint, while a treadmill wins on calories burned per minute, bone-strengthening weight-bearing exercise, and running fitness. If your goals are weight loss with low injury risk and easy consistency, the bike is the safer bet. If you are a runner or want the highest possible burn and your joints can take the impact, the treadmill edges ahead. But here is the part every comparison tiptoes around: the best machine is the one you will actually use months from now, so read to the end before you decide. In this article The quick verdict (comparison table) Which burns more calories? Which is easier on your joints? Which builds more strength? Space, noise, and living with it Which should you choose? The factor that actually decides it FAQ Stationary bike vs treadmill: the quick verdict Both are excellent cardio machines and neither is a wrong answer. Here is how they stack up on the factors that actually matter when you are choosing one for your home. Factor Stationary bike Treadmill Calorie burn per minute High Slightly higher Joint impact Low, non weight-bearing Higher, especially running Bone density benefit Limited Yes, weight-bearing Muscles worked Quads, glutes, hamstrings Fuller body plus core and balance Footprint Compact (roughly 3.5 by 2 ft) Larger, needs run-off room Noise Quiet (around 60 dB) Louder footfalls and motor Best for beginners and sore joints Yes, seated and stable Good, with walking or incline Best for runners No Yes Which burns more calories, a bike or a treadmill? The treadmill wins this one, but by less than you might think. Because running is weight-bearing and uses more muscle, it burns slightly more per minute. Research on indoor machines puts running at roughly 8 to 11 calories a minute and stationary cycling at about 8 to 10.5. In practice, a 150-pound person might burn around 530 calories in an hour of running versus about 480 cycling. That gap is real but small, and it disappears the moment intensity enters the picture. A hard interval session on a bike will out-burn an easy jog every time. What actually moves the needle for weight loss is total effort over weeks, not which machine has a slightly higher number on paper. For the bigger picture, see our guide to the best workout for weight loss . The machine with the bigger calorie number only wins if you keep showing up to use it. Which is easier on your joints? This is the bike's biggest edge. Cycling is non weight-bearing, so your knees, hips, and ankles are not absorbing the repeated impact of running. Harvard Health notes cycling builds strength and aerobic fitness with far less joint stress than higher-impact cardio. If you are coming back from injury, managing arthritis, carrying extra weight, or just want cardio that does not leave you aching the next day, the bike is the gentler choice. The treadmill's impact is not all bad news, though. Weight-bearing exercise is exactly what strengthens bones, which matters more as you age. Walking at an incline is a smart middle ground: it keeps impact modest while still delivering the bone and calorie benefits of being on your feet. Low-impact pick Aviron Fit Bike S Whisper-quiet, compact, and gentle on the joints, with games, classes, and scenic rides that make the minutes vanish. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available Shop the Fit Bike S → Which builds more strength? The treadmill works a wider range of muscles. Running or incline walking recruits your quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves, and core, and the constant balancing adds stabilizer work a seated bike does not. That broader activation is a genuine treadmill advantage. The bike answers back with resistance. Turn it up and every pedal stroke becomes strength work for your quads, glutes, and hamstrings, without any pounding. On the Fit Bike S, with 160 resistance levels that can auto-adjust, you can make a ride as light or as leg-burning as you want, which is why the same machine still challenges you a year in. Add resistance and a bike becomes leg strength training with none of the impact. Space, noise, and living with it at home This is where the bike quietly wins the practical argument. A stationary bike like the Fit Bike S has a compact footprint of roughly 3.5 by 2 feet and runs at around 60 decibels, about the level of a normal conversation, so early mornings and shared-wall apartments are fair game. A treadmill needs more room, both for the deck itself and for safe run-off space behind it, and it has more moving parts and heavier footfalls, so it is louder. None of that is a dealbreaker if you have the space and want to run, but it is worth measuring your room and picturing the noise before you buy. If a walking-focused machine is on your list, our walking pad vs treadmill guide breaks that choice down too. Runner's pick Aviron Victory Treadmill Weight-bearing cardio with incline, speed, and the same game-powered classes, scenic routes, and challenges. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available Shop the Victory Treadmill → Which should you choose? Match the machine to your body, your goals, and your space. Choose a stationary bike if you: Want low-impact cardio that is kind to your knees, hips, and back Are a beginner, a senior, or coming back from injury Have limited space or noise-sensitive neighbors Care most about consistent weight loss without soreness sidelining you Choose a treadmill if you: Are training for a run, a race, or want to keep your running fitness Want the bone-strengthening benefit of weight-bearing exercise Prefer walking, jogging, and incline work over cycling Have the floor space and do not share a wall at 6 a.m. The factor that actually decides it Notice that every honest comparison, including this one, ends up in the same place: pick the one you will enjoy enough to keep using. That is not a cop-out. It is the whole ballgame. The machine that burns 5% more calories is worthless if it becomes a clothes rack by month two, and that fear is real for both bikes and treadmills. It was never a willpower problem. Traditional equipment was built boring, so you stare at a wall while a timer crawls, and your phone was engineered to be far more interesting. Boring loses that fight every time. That is the entire idea behind Aviron: instead of bolting a screen onto a dull machine, the workout is the game. You pedal or run to race, chase scores, ride and jog scenic routes, or take coached classes, with fresh content every month. It is why Aviron reports 92% of its members are still working out a year later, the only stat that matters if you have quit before. Whichever you pick, that is the difference between a purchase and a habit. New to structured riding? Start with our stationary bike benefits guide. Bike or treadmill, the winner is whichever one you look forward to using. ★★★★★ "I have exercise and stress induced asthma and extreme ADHD, so working out is hell on earth. I actually use this bike. Multiple times per day. That's the best review I can give. I'm using it, and that's a miracle." Scarlet Lewis · Verified Buyer Frequently asked questions Is a stationary bike or treadmill better for weight loss? Both work well. Treadmills burn slightly more calories per minute, but stationary bikes are low-impact, so many people can ride longer and more often without soreness. Since weight loss comes down to consistent total effort plus a calorie deficit, the better machine is the one you will use most days. Which is better for bad knees, a bike or a treadmill? A stationary bike. Cycling is non weight-bearing, so it puts far less stress on your knees than running. If you prefer a treadmill, stick to walking, ideally at an incline, and keep the pace moderate to protect your joints. Do you burn more calories on a bike or a treadmill? On a treadmill, slightly, because running is weight-bearing and uses more muscle. Estimates put running near 8 to 11 calories a minute and cycling around 8 to 10.5. The difference is small and easily erased by riding at higher intensity or with intervals. Is a bike or treadmill better for losing belly fat? Neither targets belly fat directly, since you cannot spot-reduce. Both burn overall body fat, and belly fat comes off as you stay in a calorie deficit. Choose the machine you will use consistently and add some intervals for a bigger burn. Is a stationary bike or treadmill better for beginners and seniors? The stationary bike is usually the easier, safer start. You are seated and stable, with no balance or fall risk, and you control the effort precisely. A treadmill is still a great option for beginners who prefer walking, especially with a gentle incline. Not sure? Try it before you commit. Bring the Fit Bike S or Victory Treadmill home and ride the games, classes, and scenic routes for yourself. If it does not earn its spot, send it back. title: Sprouts Farmers Market Opens New Store in Buckeye, Arizona
body_text: Grand Opening Will Kick Off on July 24, Weekend of Activities Planned Sprouts Farmers Market has announced it will open a new store in Buckeye, Arizona on Friday, July 24, located at 20975 W. Roosevelt St., Buckeye, AZ near the Verrado master-planned community. A ribbon-cutting will take place on Friday at 6:45 a.m. and the doors to the store will open at 7 a.m. “One of the things we’ve consistently heard from residents is the desire for specialty grocery options in Buckeye, and we’re excited to welcome Sprouts Farmers Market and deliver on that request,” said Buckey Mayor Eric Orsborn.” This project brings fresh, healthy food choices, creates new jobs and continues to expand the shopping amenities that enhance the quality of life for our residents.” As one of the largest and fastest-growing specialty retailers of fresh, natural and organic food in the United States, Sprouts helps people live and eat better. Stepping into Sprouts, shoppers can expect an experience rooted in freshness, quality and wellness – with delicious discoveries down every aisle. From everyday essentials to specialty finds, Sprouts makes healthy living accessible and affordable with: Fresh Produce – Sprouts offers the season’s freshest, most delicious produce at the heart of the store, sourced in partnership with local and regional farmers. Healthy Proteins – Sprouts sells a wide variety of protein offerings, including No Antibiotics Ever chicken, 100% grass-fed beef, sustainably-sourced seafood and vegetarian and vegan offerings for the widest assortment of high-quality protein. Fast, fresh lunch solutions including: $5 Sushi Wednesdays – Sprouts rolls fresh sushi daily in-store and offers $5 sushi specials every Wednesday. Famous $5 Sandwiches – Sprouts’ Deli features build-your-own and grab-and-go sandwiches starting at just $4.99 featuring Sprouts Brand Deli Meats that are free from preservatives, nitrates and sliced daily. The Deli also offers convenient ready-to-eat meals and heat and eat prepared foods. Sprouts Wellness Bowls – Fresh, flavorful and ready-to-eat meals made daily in-store, packed with protein and perfect for a quick, healthy meal, starting at just $8.99. Wellness Products – An assortment of more than 7,000 vitamins, supplements and wellness products awaits you at Sprouts with wellness experts in every store offering a wealth of knowledge to guide customers on their health and nutrition journeys. Bulk Department – Sprouts’ bulk department features hundreds of bins and barrels brimming with freshly roasted coffee beans, rice, nuts, dried fruits, granolas, trail mixes, baking essentials, spices and sweets; scoop up as much or as little as needed. All bulk products are free from artificial colors and artificial flavors. Sprouts Rewards – Sprouts Rewards makes shopping more rewarding! Members earn points on every in-store and online purchase, unlock exclusive events and offers, and enjoy more ways to live and eat better. The program is free to join; points start after your first purchase, and it’s available at all Sprouts locations nationwide. To kick off the grand opening weekend, Sprouts is hosting a series of onsite activities. From Friday, July 24 through Sunday, July 26, a variety of activities will celebrate the grand opening offering fun for the whole family and will last all weekend long. The first 200 shoppers on Friday and Saturday will receive a free reusable tote. Plus, the first 400 guests on Friday will receive a free long stem rose courtesy of Falcon Farms Floral. Inside the store, shoppers can sample products from Sprouts. Shoppers can receive 20% off their purchase once over the grand opening weekend when they sign up for a Sprouts Rewards account. Visit Sprouts.com/rewards to join Sprouts Rewards. Shoppers can enter their phone number or scan their barcode in-store or shop online using promo code BUCKGO20. For more information and terms and conditions on the promotions, visit www.Sprouts.com/buckeye . Sprouts Farmers Market is invested in serving the communities where it operates. It works with local and regional farmers like Duncan Family Farms and Blue Sky Organic Farms to source local produce. Through Sprouts’ Food Rescue program this store will donate groceries that are no longer fit for sale but remain perfectly edible and nutrient rich to the St. Marys Food Bank . This location will be open daily from 7 a.m. until 10 p.m. For more information and to sign up to win a $500 Sprouts gift card, visit www.Sprouts.com/buckeye About Sprouts Farmers Market, Inc. Sprouts Farmers Market is one of the largest and fastest growing specialty retailers of fresh, natural and organic food in the United States. Sprouts helps people live and eat better with fresh produce at the heart of the store and delicious discoveries for every dietary lifestyle. Always foraging for what’s fresh and innovative, Sprouts offers a carefully curated assortment of products that inspire wellness naturally, including organic, gluten-free, plant-based and non-GMO favorites. Headquartered in Phoenix, AZ, Sprouts employs approximately 36,000 team members and operates more than 480 stores in 25 states nationwide. To learn more about Sprouts and the role it plays in its communities, visit Sprouts.com/about .
